sections.html:
Your options in Sunrise are an agent listing, a sale you run yourself, or a cash offer, and each one runs into the city's permit rules and Broward County's records. Sunrise is a planned city on the western edge of Broward County, with more than 98,000 residents and a lot of highway access, which buyers like to see in a listing.

Fast sales hinge on documents. Pull together the deed, any homeowners association papers, permit records and a recent tax bill, and you can answer a buyer's questions in a day instead of a week.

Sunrise uses two tracks. Work that changes a building's footprint or exterior goes through Broward County and the city's Community Development Department. Smaller jobs go straight to the Building Division. Re-roofing, interior renovation, fencing, interior plumbing or electrical repairs and AC changeouts skip Planning and Development review.

Steps in a Sunrise permit application
StepWhat happens
1. Choose where to fileDemolition, additions, alterations and new construction need Broward County approval first, then city review
2. File the applicationThe city issues a Control Number used for the whole approval
3. Correct plansApplicant is notified of corrections; Wednesday mornings are Professional Day
4. Receive the permitIssued after structural, electrical, plumbing, mechanical and fire approvals; fees due at submittal

The Building Division's number is (954) 572-2354, and applications can be filed electronically. If a previous owner added a room or screen enclosure, ask the division whether it was permitted and finaled.

sections.h2: Permit problems that slow a sale
sections.html:
Unfinished permits and unpermitted additions cause the most trouble, because they turn up in a buyer's title or inspection review.

  • Additions or garage conversions that changed the exterior, which need both county and city sign-off.
  • Roof, AC and plumbing work done by a contractor without a final inspection.
  • Fences and other work done without any permit.

If you find a gap, you can close it before listing or disclose it and let the price reflect it. A cash buyer will usually accept either, but get the terms in writing. Do not assume your own report is enough, since lenders and title companies pull their own records.

The Broward property appraiser sets your home's value as of January 1, and bills come from the tax collector in November. A closing in the second half of the year means prorating the full-year bill. Selling ends your Save Our Homes cap, and on the following January 1 the buyer is assessed at just value.

The homestead exemption can remove up to $50,000 if the owner files by March 1 and had made the home a permanent residence by January 1. Owners 65 or older may qualify for an extra local exemption if the city or county has enacted one and income limits are met, so ask the Broward County property appraiser which apply to your address.

Paying in November earns the printed 4 percent discount, which drops one point each month through February.

sections.h2: Stamp tax and recording on a Sunrise deed
sections.html:
Deeds in Broward are taxed at the usual state rate, 70 cents on each $100 of consideration, and Miami-Dade stands alone with a different structure. The clerk takes the tax when the deed is recorded, and everyone on the document is liable.

Under section 28.24 the clerk charges $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 afterward, plus extra per-page fees. Title insurance and lien payoffs come on top.

Before signing, ask any buyer for a written cost split covering stamp tax, title and recording, and whether the offer depends on an inspection.

Compare them on timeline, certainty and net proceeds. Listing puts the house in front of the most buyers, at the cost of showings, inspection haggling and the chance a loan falls through. Cash gives up some price in return for a faster close with fewer surprises.

  • Get every buyer's closing date in writing.
  • Ask what happens if their inspection finds permit gaps.
  • Settle who orders and pays for the title search.
  • Ask whether proof of funds is available on request.

A Sunrise home with a finished permit file, a clear tax picture and a deed ready to record is easy to price either way. With a mortgage on the house, get a payoff letter first. It shows the lowest offer you can afford to accept.

sections.h2: Documents to gather before you call buyers
sections.html:
Sellers who show up with paper get better, faster offers. A short folder is enough, and most of it is already in your files.

  • The recorded deed and any survey.
  • Your latest Broward County tax bill and proof of any exemption.
  • Permit records for the roof, AC, plumbing, additions and fences, with final inspection dates.
  • Homeowners association rules, fees and contact details, if there is an association.
  • A payoff letter for each mortgage or lien.

If a permit is missing, call the Building Division before you list. Staff can tell you whether it was never filed, filed but not finaled, or sent to the county first because the work changed the exterior. Knowing which one it is lets you pick between closing the gap and pricing it in.

sections.h2: Pricing a house with permit gaps
sections.html:
A gap does not stop a sale, but it changes who will pay what you ask. Conventional buyers rely on lenders and title companies, and those pull their own permit records, so a gap that you skip mentioning will surface anyway. Cash buyers usually accept an open permit and take the cost off the offer.

When you compare offers, ask each buyer to say in writing how an open permit, an unpermitted fence or a garage conversion would affect the price and the closing date. That answer tells you whether it is cheaper to finish the paperwork yourself or sell as-is.

sections.h2: From signed contract to recorded deed
sections.html:
Once an offer is accepted, a title agent searches the records for mortgages, liens and unpaid taxes. Anything found is paid from your proceeds at closing. You sign the deed, the closing agent submits it to the Broward County clerk, and stamp tax and recording fees are collected at that moment.

  1. Order payoff letters for every loan or lien.
  2. Ask the tax collector about the balance and proration for the year.
  3. Finish or disclose any open permit.
  4. Request homeowners association documents if the home sits in a community with an association.

If the house is vacant, plan the key handoff and utility transfers for closing day. Ask the closing agent for a written settlement statement ahead of time, and read each line, including stamp tax, recording, title insurance and any tax proration, so that nothing at the table is a surprise. Keep a copy of the recorded deed once the clerk returns it.

faqs.q: Does Sunrise have its own building division?
faqs.a: Yes. The City of Sunrise Building Division handles permits at (954) 572-2354. Work that changes a building's exterior or footprint also goes through Community Development, and larger jobs need Broward County approval first.

faqs.q: Is a permit required to replace a roof in Sunrise?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. Re-roofing goes straight to the Building Division. Confirm with the division before work begins and keep the final inspection record.

faqs.q: What if I find an open permit on my Sunrise house?
faqs.a: Either finish it with the Building Division before listing or disclose it and let the price reflect it. Cash buyers often accept open permits at a lower figure.

faqs.q: Is the documentary stamp rate different in Broward County?
faqs.a: No. Broward charges the usual 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and Miami-Dade is the sole exception.

faqs.q: Will my homestead exemption stay with the house?
faqs.a: No. Your buyer files a new application by March 1, and the sale resets the assessment to just value.
